cards.front: Recall a key point about Crime, Deviance & Social Control
cards.back: Crime: an act that breaks the law and is punishable by the state. Deviance: behaviour that violates social norms. Not all deviance is crime (dyeing your hair an unusual colour is deviant but legal) and not all crime is deviant (speeding is illegal but widely accepted). The boundary between crime and deviance changes over time (homosexuality was a crime until 1967 in the UK).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Crime, Deviance & Social Control
cards.back: Deviance is socially constructed: what counts as deviant varies across cultures and time periods. Example: drink-driving was once socially acceptable but is now both deviant and criminal; smoking in public places was normal but is now deviant and restricted. Becker: 'deviance is not a quality of the act but of the response of others to the act' - the same behaviour can be deviant in one context but not another.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Crime, Deviance & Social Control
cards.back: Formal social control: carried out by official agencies (police, courts, prisons). Based on written laws and formal sanctions (arrest, imprisonment, fines). The criminal justice system detects, prosecutes and punishes crime.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Crime, Deviance & Social Control
cards.back: Informal social control: carried out by social groups (family, peers, community). Based on unwritten norms and informal sanctions (gossip, ostracism, disapproval, shame). Families socialise children into norms; communities enforce conformity through social pressure.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Crime, Deviance & Social Control
cards.back: Social control and power: Marxists argue laws reflect ruling class interests. Chambliss: laws protecting private property serve the bourgeoisie. Selective enforcement: the poor are more likely to be policed and prosecuted (Reiman: 'the rich get richer and the poor get prison'). White-collar crime (fraud, tax evasion) causes far more financial damage than street crime but is less rigorously policed.

cards.front: What should you know about sociology exam tips?
cards.back: When discussing crime and deviance, always: distinguish crime from deviance, explain how deviance is socially constructed, and consider whether definitions of crime reflect power relations rather than objective harm.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Something is deviant because it is naturally wrong, regardless of what society thinks. Correct: Deviance is socially constructed - what is deviant in one society may be normal in another, and what is deviant at one time may become acceptable later.
